The fight was a blizzard of glass and metal. Tobias stood in the dark garage, the driver’s door of his sedan creased like a soda can. Ivy leaned against the wall, her breath a cheap-wine fog. “It’s just a car,” she said. He didn’t answer. She walked out into the March sleet, and he let the door slam.

---

At the drive-in, Ivy pressed her cheek against the cool of his shoulder. The screen flickered blue across her face. “Don’t let me fall asleep,” she whispered, and he kissed the crown of her head. The film ended with credits rolling over a highway. She was already dreaming.

---

A week later, Ivy stood at the counter of the memory-erasure clinic. “Remove all of him,” she told Dr. Hallam, sliding a photo of Tobias across the desk. The technician, Dell, watched from a doorway, a cigarette burning forgotten between his fingers.

---

They shared a bowl of noodles at the shop with the cracked lanterns. Steam rose between them like a curtain. She slurped and laughed, and Tobias pulled a strand of noodle from her chin. “I’ll never forget this,” she said. He believed her.

---

Tobias appeared at the clinic the following morning. “I want what she had,” he said to Hallam. He boxed everything: the pressed-flower bookmarks, the Polaroid of her sleeping on the beach, the scarf she’d left in his drawer. Each object a tag on a memory map.

---

Fog lay on the river that winter. She was learning to skate. Her ankles wobbled, and he caught her, both of them laughing into the white air. She carved a lopsided heart into the ice with her toe. “That’s us,” she said. He traced it with his finger until the grooves filled with snow.

---

The technicians Dell and Peck plugged Tobias into the machine. Peck pocketed a scarf—the same one from the box—to use on Ivy later. Inside his own skull, Tobias watched the ugliest memories dissolve like aspirin in water. He reached for the good ones, tried to tape Ivy into scenes she’d never been. The map warped. Dell and the receptionist Rosa got high on his bed, lost the thread. Hallam arrived to re-map, but Rosa kissed him, and his wife appeared from a corridor, her face unreadable. “She already had that erased,” the wife said. Rosa’s own affair was a zero.

In the last surviving memory, the empty house on the shore. Wind through salt-rotted windows. Ivy stood barefoot on the floorboards. “This is where we met,” she said. Then she added, “Meet me at the beach.” Tobias tried to hold the image, but it frayed.

---

The first day at that same beach: a bonfire, a stolen key to the unoccupied house. She’d found him in the crowd, held up a bottle of wine. “You go first,” she’d said, and they’d crept up the dune together. Her hand in his. That first, impossible touch.

---

The erasure completed. Tobias woke in his own bed with a headache and no name for the emptiness. He called in sick—an impulse he couldn’t explain—took the train to the coast, and walked onto the frozen sand. She was there. They drove back to the city, and she invited him up. On her table, a package: Rosa had mailed the clinic’s tapes to every patient. They sat in the dark and listened to their own voices tearing each other apart—the dented car, the withheld apologies, the word “goodbye.” After the tape ended, Ivy ran to the bathroom. She came back with wet cheeks. “We could try,” she said. He looked at her. He didn’t know why his chest ached, or why the empty house on the shore felt like the beginning. But he nodded.

The snow globe left his hand in the same instant the word did. "Bluebell." The glass struck the parquet of Silvermount's great hall, and the mirrors that lined every wall threw the shatter back at him a hundred times over. Emmett Rusk died with his fingers still reaching for the glittering shards.

He had been a boy when his mother signed him over to the banker Barrow, a defaulted lodger's mine deed making the family suddenly rich and suddenly disposable. The boy drove his sled straight into Barrow's stomach, and was taken east anyway, away from the mining boarding house and the parents who had sold him. He never forgave the fortune. He only took it.

On his twenty-fifth birthday, Emmett told Barrow that of all the holdings, he wanted the failing newspaper. He installed his manager Marsh and his friend Devlin, printed a signed statement of principles on the front page, hired away the entire staff of the rival paper, and threw a party with a brass band and a chorus line. He returned from a buying trip abroad engaged to Adele, the governor's niece. The breakfast-table scenes followed: two people reading separate newspapers, the silence between them hardening like poured concrete.

The newsreel obituary ran after his death, recapping the public life—the paper, the gubernatorial campaign, the marriage to the opera singer who had no voice—and closed without once explaining his last word. The reporter Nash was sent to find out what "Bluebell" meant. A drunk Nora turned him away at a seaside nightclub, the salt wind pulling at her hair.

Nash went looking anyway. He read Barrow's memoir, which described the sled incident and the boy's silent fury. He interviewed Marsh, who remembered the principles and the party. Devlin, who remembered asking for a transfer after the election loss, and the review he'd written drunk and Emmett had finished, printed, and fired him for. Nora, who remembered the opera debut that was a humiliation, the poison she swallowed rather than sing again, and the way Emmett finally let her stop. Colm the butler, who remembered the joyless beach picnic and the quarrel, and Nora packing her bags.

The meeting with Nora had begun mid-campaign, the mud on Emmett's coat, her rooms in secret. Halloran, the party boss, had brought Adele there to threaten exposure. Emmett refused to withdraw, lost the election, lost Devlin, lost the marriage. He married Nora and forced her onto the stage. He shut her away in the half-finished palace called Silvermount, where she worked jigsaw puzzles in the vast empty hall. After the beach picnic, she left him. He wrecked her bedroom, found the glass snow globe, murmured "Bluebell," and carried it past the endless mirrors.

Nash concluded that no single word explains a life. Behind him, workmen shoveled a sled marked *Bluebell* into the furnace, the wood blackening, the paint blistering, the name curling into ash.

I was an insomniac product-recall investigator. The only thing that let me sleep was crying at support groups for diseases I did not have. Then Ada Vey started attending the same groups, and her obvious faking destroyed my release. She was beautiful and hollow, and she mimicked tears with the precision of a machine.

I would later put a gun in my own mouth and shoot myself through the cheek to kill Rex. But that was after I understood that he and I were the same person. Before that, I met a soap salesman named Rex Marrow on a business flight. I pocketed his card. My flat and all its catalogue furniture were destroyed in an explosion, and I called Rex. He took me into a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district.

Outside a bar he asked me to hit him as hard as I could. We beat each other bloody in the car park. What started as two men brawling hardened into a weekly basement club with its own rules, pulling in more and more members. Ada overdosed; Rex brought her back to the derelict house, and they began a loud affair I could not stand. He rendered fat stolen from a cosmetic surgery clinic into soap and sold it back to the department stores at eighty dollars a bar. He burned my hand with lye and held me there, refusing to let me retreat into meditation. I blackmailed my employer into paying me to stay away, using my own beaten face as evidence.

Rex turned the club into an organisation he called Havoc, filling the house with shaven recruits who took orders and vandalised corporate property. He steered the car into oncoming traffic, let it roll, and then disappeared. A member named Ogden was shot dead on an operation, and I started trying to shut the whole thing down. Travelling city to city, I found identical clubs everywhere and men who greeted me as Rex Marrow. I worked out that he and I were the same person, and that he had been acting while I slept. Ada confirmed that she had been sleeping with me, not with a separate man.

I discovered that Havoc had mined the towers of the debt-record companies and tried to defuse the charges. Rex beat me down a stairwell in one of the towers. I put a gun in my own mouth and shot myself through the cheek to kill him. Ada was delivered to the tower by the shaven recruits, and we held hands at the window as the buildings came down.

The wound healed. I still have the scar. I sleep now, sometimes, but I do not cry in support groups anymore. I know what I am.

Aaron's chest rises with a rhythm that does not belong to him. The pool water shimmers, and he watches Lena on the far side, her towel held tight across her body, the absence of small voices visible in the way she glances at the empty shallow end.

Wes's hands shake as he strips the sheets from Room 14. The Bible stays shut in the nightstand drawer. He hasn't opened it in months. His shoulder aches where the bullet passed through, a reminder he was told to run and did not.

Lena sits in the hospital corridor while a doctor speaks. The words do not form sentences. Doug. The girls. The crossing. A pickup truck. She nods at nothing.

Aaron signs the consent form. Della watches him with flat eyes. "Do it," she says. The cold room at the sperm bank hums around them. His failing heart stutters.

Wes coaches the boys at third base. He yells, catches himself, drops to one knee and prays. Nita watches from the minivan, knuckles white on the wheel, afraid of his god and his temper in equal measure.

The pickup hits them. Doug's body arcs over the hood. The girls do not scream. Wes's foot finds the gas, then the brake, then the gas again. He drives off. He turns back. He flees.

Lena's dealer knows her voice by now. She doesn't have to explain what she needs.

The private investigator slides a folder across the table. Aaron opens it. Lena Ward. Suburban. Two daughters. Widow. His hand presses to his sternum, to the heart that beats in time with a dead man's memory.

Della's hand rests on her stomach. Aaron's hand rests on his chest. "I don't want it," he says. She does not argue. She does not cry.

Wes walks into the police station. The desk sergeant looks up from his coffee. Wes says the words. The handcuffs close with a sound he knows.

Lena and Aaron meet at the pool. She laughs at something he says, and Doug's heart—his heart—beats faster in his chest.

Aaron tells her. Her face changes. She throws the glass. It shatters against the wall. Then she is in his arms, and he holds her, and she holds him back.

Wes is released early. Nita's face when he tells her. He leaves the faith at the door like a coat he no longer wants.

Lena's voice on the phone is quiet. "Kill him." Aaron buys the gun. The salesman asks about his day. Aaron says fine.

The motel. Wes's pickup in the lot. Aaron's hand shakes. He fires. Wes's shoulder blooms red. "Run," Aaron says.

Wes does not run. He follows them. He finds their room. He looks at Aaron. "Finish it."

Aaron puts the barrel in his mouth. Lena screams. Wes moves. The gun goes off—not at Wes.

The hospital. Aaron's chest opens again. Doug's heart fails. Wes walks home to Nita and the boys. Lena, pregnant with a child that will never know its father's face, walks home alone.

Della gets the news. She does not call anyone. She sits with her hand on her stomach, and she does not think about the heart that stopped, or the one that beat inside it, or the man who carried it and could not carry the weight.

In a flat overlooking the street, an old man said to a younger one, “Nothing survives time.” Below, police were handcuffing two men and carrying them from a club. The younger man watched. The old man nodded. “Even memory dissolves.”

The cuffs clicked around Cort’s wrists. Jonah stood beside him, blood on his knuckles, his sleeves wet with it. They had been pulled apart from the body on the floor—a man whose face was no longer a face, crushed by a fire extinguisher. The real Adder had watched from a few feet away as Jonah beat the wrong man. Cort had grabbed that man first, had his arm snapped for the mistake. Then Jonah had swung.

Earlier, outside the party, two men had offered to sell Cort the rapist’s name. They steered him and Jonah toward the Pit. Cort was drunk, still high, his mind a fog of guilt and rage. He had wanted to find the man who hurt Lise.

But before that, Cort and Jonah had come out of the party to find Lise being loaded into an ambulance. Her head was bleeding, her dress torn. Cort vomited on the sidewalk. Jonah stood frozen. The paramedics worked quickly.

Before the ambulance, Lise had walked into a pedestrian underpass rather than cross the busy road. She had seen a pimp—the Adder—beating a transsexual woman. He turned on her. He raped her. He beat her head against the concrete. A passer-by glimpsed them and backed away. No one helped.

Before the underpass, Lise had left the party alone. Cort had gotten steadily drunk and high, then started pursuing other women. She watched him press himself against a redhead at the bar. Disgusted, she walked out. She didn’t want to see it.

Before the party, the three of them—Lise, Cort, Jonah—had ridden the underground together. They argued cheerfully about sex and about Cort’s drinking. Jonah teased Lise about Cort’s bad habits. Cort laughed. Lise held Jonah’s hand for a moment, then let go. They were on their way to the party.

Before that, Lise had sat in a park among sprinklers and playing children. One hand rested on her stomach. She watched a toddler stumble through a spray of water. She did not smile. She did not frown. She simply waited.

Before the park, alone in the flat, Lise had taken a pregnancy test. She watched the two lines appear. Positive. She put the test on the bathroom counter and stood very still for a long time.

Before the test, Lise had lain in bed with Cort. She described a recurring dream of a red tunnel—a narrow, pulsing corridor that always ended in darkness. Cort teased her about her ex-boyfriend Jonah. “You still dream about him?” he asked. She rolled her eyes. “It’s not about Jonah.” Cort laughed and pulled her closer. “Sure it isn’t.” She laughed too. The dream was always the same. The tunnel was warm. She never reached the end.

Helicopters sprayed the city through the night, their rotors shuddering over every neighbourhood. The noise was a dull hum beneath the Hartigans’ house as Doctor Neil Hartigan and his wife Bess, a painter, got ready for a dinner party. Bess touched up her lipstick; Neil loosened his tie. They did not speak of the tremors that had begun to trouble the city’s foundations.

A few miles away, the baker Otto Kemp took an order for a birthday cake for a boy called Charlie Rill. He wrote the name in his ledger, flour dusting his fingers. That same morning, Charlie was knocked down by a car driven by a waitress called Rhona on his way to school. He got up, walked home, insisted he was fine. His parents, Grant and Elaine, believed him.

But that night Charlie collapsed into a coma. At the hospital, Grant and Elaine kept vigil. The machines beeped. Grant’s estranged father, Duff, turned up unannounced and confessed an affair from decades ago, weeping in the waiting room. The family ignored him. Unpaid and ignored, Otto started making anonymous menacing phone calls to the Rill household. No one answered.

Across town, telephone-sex worker Cheryl talked men through their fantasies from her living room while her husband Stu seethed beside her. He said nothing. One weekend, Stu and three friends drove out to fish. They found a young woman’s body face down in the river. They tethering her to the bank with a rope and carried on fishing for two more days before telling anyone. When Vern’s wife Iris, a party clown, learned what they had done, she was disgusted. She scrubbed her face and did not perform that night.

The singer Vida performed nightly in a club while her cellist daughter Bee played alone at home. Bee’s music was thin and sad. Meanwhile, Officer Rowe, cheating on his wife Peg with a woman called Nan, abandoned the family dog to cover one of his lies. He drove the dog to the outskirts and left it tied to a fence. Nan’s ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot, learned she had a new man and sawed her furniture to pieces. He did it methodically, blade through wood.

Ike and Dot house-sat for the Hartigans while they were at the dinner party. They photographed Dot made up as a beaten corpse, fake blood on her face, sprawled on the Persian rug. At the dinner party, Bess admitted to a long-ago nude modelling session and an affair. Neil made a scene, sending wine across the tablecloth. The guests left early.

Charlie died in the hospital. Grant and Elaine went to the bakery to confront Otto. He fed them warm bread and grieved with them, his hands shaking. They ate in silence.

Bee found her mother drowsy in the armchair, closed the garage door, and started the car engine. She sat in the driver’s seat and let the fumes take her. The car ran until the tank was dry.

At a picnic in the hills, Stu smashed a young woman’s head with a rock. He did it quickly, then sat down and ate a sandwich. His friends watched.

Then a tremor shook the entire city. The helicopters faltered, the hospital lights flickered, the bakery shelves rattled. Every death and every wreck was folded into one evening bulletin: the body in the river, the girl in the garage, the woman on the hillside, the abandoned dog, the shattered furniture, the coma, the affair, the party, the photos, the phone calls, the cake order, the paint and the blood and the bread. The bulletin read like a ledger, like a recipe, like a confession. The city settled into its new shape, still trembling.

Shaved and in clean clothes, Cardo left his money for Perla on the kitchen counter. He walked out into the wasteland with Tigre at his heel, the dog’s ribs still showing through its coat. In his mind he saw the answering machine he’d filled with a confession, the photograph he’d taken of his daughter while she slept. He remembered the day he’d watched his estranged wife’s burial from a distance, then followed Perla home. He remembered chaining Sergio in the lair instead of killing him, then bringing Elian face to face with his brother and leaving a loaded pistol between them. He had taken money from both. And before that, he had dragged a bleeding rottweiler out of a wrecked car at a junction, the dog’s leg shattered. He had nursed it back to health among his own pack of strays. But when he returned one afternoon to find Tigre had killed every other dog in the yard, Cardo put a gun to the animal’s head and could not fire.

Ruben stood at his brother Nestor’s funeral and watched Alma hold the baby. The grave was still open. “Come with me,” he whispered. She shook her head and turned away. He remembered the cramped house they’d all shared, Nestor robbing a pharmacy by night and beating Alma at home. Ruben had started pressing her to run away, then discovered that Nestor’s rottweiler, Tigre, killed other dogs on sight. He had entered the dog in local fights and won steadily. With the money he paid two thugs to beat Nestor, but Nestor responded by taking Alma, the baby, and Ruben’s hidden savings. Ruben was left with nothing but the dog. In a last fight the promoter Chaco shot Tigre in the ring. Ruben stabbed him and fled with his friend Pipo. They ran a red light at speed and ploughed into a car—a woman at the wheel. He had seen her face just before impact, the same face that stared down from a billboard above the city.

Celine Vaz woke in hospital with her leg pinned together. Her lover Hector had walked out on his wife and daughters and moved her into a new flat facing her own billboard. She had thought it was a fresh start. But her lapdog Chispa was lost somewhere in the flat. Hector tore up the floorboards searching while Celine’s leg turned gangrenous. The leg was amputated. Shaved and in clean clothes, Cardo left his money for Perla on the kitchen counter. He walked out into the wasteland with Tigre at his heel, the dog’s ribs still showing through its coat. In his mind he saw the answering machine he’d filled with a confession, the photograph he’d taken of his daughter while she slept. He remembered the day he’d watched his estranged wife’s burial from a distance, then followed Perla home. He remembered chaining Sergio in the lair instead of killing him, then bringing Elian face to face with his brother and leaving a loaded pistol between them. He had taken money from both. And before that, he had dragged a bleeding rottweiler out of a wrecked car at a junction, the dog’s leg shattered. He had nursed it back to health among his own pack of strays. But when he returned one afternoon to find Tigre had killed every other dog in the yard, Cardo put a gun to the animal’s head and could not fire.

Ruben stood at his brother Nestor’s funeral and watched Alma hold the baby. The grave was still open. “Come with me,” he whispered. She shook her head and turned away. He remembered the cramped house they’d all shared, Nestor robbing a pharmacy by night and beating Alma at home. Ruben had started pressing her to run away, then discovered that Nestor’s rottweiler, Tigre, killed other dogs on sight. He had entered the dog in local fights and won steadily. With the money he paid two thugs to beat Nestor, but Nestor responded by taking Alma, the baby, and Ruben’s hidden savings. Ruben was left with nothing but the dog. In a last fight the promoter Chaco shot Tigre in the ring. Ruben stabbed him and fled with his friend Pipo. They ran a red light at speed and ploughed into a car—a woman at the wheel. He had seen her face just before impact, the same face that stared down from a billboard above the city.

She had thought it was a fresh start. But her lapdog Chispa was lost somewhere in the flat. Hector tore up the floorboards searching while Celine’s leg turned gangrenous. The leg was amputated. Soon after, the billboard carrying her image was taken down. She never saw the dog again.

He knew it would end this way. The beam weapon’s heat was familiar, a warmth he had felt before the first breath. He addressed the crowd, the words tasting of old dust and wet wool, and then the light took him.

On the alien planet, the actress wept in the enclosure beside him. The zoo visitors drifted past, gelatinous and silent, observing them with the same curiosity he had once given to ants. They explained it to him—every moment exists at once. His birth in the industrial town, the weak child learning to cough smoke and grit, was happening now. His father’s hand on his back, the chlorine sting, the weight of water pushing him down to the concrete bottom. That moment was here, too.

The chaplain’s assistant never learned to shoot. They shipped him overseas without training, and he wandered into a field of poppies that turned into mud. The scout beat him for wanting to die, fists against his ribs, and the sound was the same as the scraping of bodies from the cellar. The city burned in one night, and the prisoners emerged from the meat locker to find the abattoir open to stars. A digger beside him vomited until his heart stopped. The scout, on the train, blamed him with a rattling breath. Gangrene had turned his leg black. “You did this,” he said, and the words stuck.

A fellow prisoner promised to kill him one day, for the scout’s sake. That promise was still true, still waiting somewhere in the stack of moments.

He went home and collapsed. The hospital bed had a plastic mattress that smelled of bleach. The patient in the next bed handed him a crumbling magazine. “Read this,” he said. The hack science fiction writer wrote about rockets and aliens, and the boy—the man—laughed, because he had already been in the zoo.

He married the optometrist’s daughter. She had a laugh like a bell, and the money bought a house with a view of the mountains. But the mountains also held the crash. The plane’s wing snapped silently against a ridge, and she died of exhaust fumes driving alone to the hospital. He walked out of the wreckage with only a bruise on his cheek. That bruise was still there, a purple memory.

The radio talk show host smiled with too many teeth. “Tell us about the fourth dimension,” she said. He tried. He spoke of the zoo, of the gelatinous beings, of how free will was a local idea, like a regional dialect. But the daughter listening at home decided he was senile. She took his affairs—the money, the house, the letters from the war—and put them in a lockbox. She did not understand that his affairs were already finished, already happening in all directions.

He sank again, that first time, lungs burning, looking up at the distorted face of his father. He was drowning. He was always drowning. The beam hit his chest, and he knew the scout’s curse had never ended. The crowd screamed, and the actress in the zoo reached through the glass, and the digger fell into the cellar, and the bodies were stacked like firewood.

Aliens. War. Marriage. Death. A boy born in a town of smoke and iron. Every moment at once, and he could not tell which came first. Neither could you.

The party was in full swing downstairs, the clink of glasses and murmur of voices rising through the floorboards. Wilder took Odile by the elbow and guided her up the narrow staircase to a bedroom that smelled of mothballs and old wood. He told her she was lovely, and she did not pull away. Below, the other guests drank on, oblivious.

They rented rooms in a quiet district soon after—two small rooms with a kitchenette. They bought linen and plates, and slowly the place took on the shape of a household. The affair had a home.

One afternoon Odile sat on the edge of the iron bed and said she was carrying her husband’s child. Wilder said nothing for a long moment, then nodded. They decided the rooms would go on exactly as before. Nothing would change.

Months later, in a hotel abroad, Emlyn—her husband—asked about a letter that had been held for her at the front desk. He recognized the handwriting. Odile confessed everything. Emlyn listened, then remarked that he had always been fonder of his friend Wilder than of his wife. He said it without rancor, as if stating a simple fact.

She returned to the rented rooms. She said nothing whatever about the trip, and the afternoon passed exactly as the others had—quiet, domestic, the kettle whistling, the light fading through the net curtains.

Emlyn took Wilder to lunch at a long restaurant. He drank steadily through the meal and baited Wilder about contemporary fiction—its pretensions, its failures. He never once mentioned what he had learned.

That evening, the three of them sat down to dinner at the married couple’s house. The two men talked of racquet games and schoolboy sport, their voices easy and familiar. Odile had no part in the talk. She watched them from across the table, a silent third.

As time went on, the rented rooms became a chore. The affair had lost its secrecy, its thrill. Wilder and Odile split the crockery one afternoon—deliberately, methodically, each piece shattering on the floorboards. Then they surrendered the lease.

Two years afterwards, in a bar, Odile found Wilder again. She told him her marriage was over. She had spent the previous night confessing everything to her husband—every detail, every meeting, every lie. She let slip, too, that Emlyn had been publishing a writer whom Wilder represented. Both men, she said, quietly detested that writer.

Wilder rang Emlyn that same evening, in a state. Emlyn came to his house. They sat across from each other in the dim living room.

“I have known for four years,” Emlyn said. “My wife told me on the trip abroad. And I never thought much of your letters either.”

Wilder looked at him. The words hung in the air—a final, quiet symmetry. Outside, the streetlights flickered on. Neither man spoke again.

The dog sat on the counter of the pet shop, its tail wagging dumbly, as the clerk wiped the slime from his palm. A diamond the size of a quail’s egg glistened in the light. Halloway and Digby stood in the doorway, their faces grey with exhaustion and something like awe. Halloway reached out and picked it up. He had no words. It had been a week of blood and fire, and now the whole cursed affair had resolved itself into a single, absurd, beautiful stone.

It had started with Solly Two Coats, who had robbed a diamond house in a northern port dressed as a pilgrim, walking out with the huge stone hidden in his robes. His cousin Marv, safe overseas, had sent word: *Bring it straight over.* So Solly had sailed south, landed in the city, and delivered the stone to the fence, Hersch. But before he could leave, his old acquaintance Grigor the Nail had told him about a bookmaker’s in the city where a fortune could be won on a fixed fight. What Solly didn’t know was that Grigor had also tipped off the pawnbrokers, Ike and Benno, that a man with a case full of money would be there.

The fight was the talk of the town. The promoters, Halloway and Digby, had sent their fighter, Pretty Sam, to buy a caravan from a camp of travellers. But the bare-knuckle fighter Finn had knocked Sam out over the deal, leaving Halloway without a man for the gang boss Coldstone’s fixed bout. Desperate, Halloway put Finn in the fight and promised Coldstone that Finn would go down in the fourth round.

Solly, unaware of any of this, walked into the bookmaker’s with his case, ready to bet on the fight. Ike, Benno, and a man named Tulley bungled the robbery. They grabbed Solly’s arm and his case, but in the chaos, they were chased off by Grigor, who had been watching. Solly was left bleeding on the floor.

That night, Finn knocked his opponent out cold in the first round. Coldstone lost a fortune, and his wrath fell on Halloway, who was beaten bloody in an alley. Meanwhile, Marv flew in, found Solly gone, and hired the bounty hunter Ledge to find him.

Grigor took Solly to a basement, cut off his arm to get the case open, and found only paper. The stone was not inside. Solly screamed, but Grigor only smiled.

Ledge traced the pawnbrokers. He shot their car to pieces and took both them and the stone, which they had found in the case—a separate, smaller stone, not the one from the north. He put them in the trunk and drove off.

Coldstone, furious about the first fight, fed Solly to his pigs and told Halloway and Digby what would happen if the second fight went wrong. They went to Finn and told him to go down in the fourth. To make sure he obeyed, Coldstone’s men burned Finn’s mother to death in her caravan.

Grigor ambushed Ledge’s car. In the shootout, Ledge, Grigor, and Benno were all killed. The car rolled into a ditch. Tulley, who had been hiding in the back, crawled out with a dog that had swallowed the diamond.

In the fourth round of the second fight, Finn knocked his opponent out again. The travellers in the crowd rose up and massacred Coldstone’s men. Halloway and Digby found Coldstone and shot him. By morning, the travellers had vanished.

The dog was found wandering, handed in at a pet shop. It coughed up the diamond. Halloway and Digby walked out with it, the stone heavy in Halloway’s pocket, the whole bloody saga reduced to a single, glittering prize.

The gun dealer laughed at Nadir's accent. "Say 'protection' again," he said, and Nadir did, and the dealer laughed harder. Sahar stood by the door with her arms crossed. When they left, she said, "He won't remember us."

But the gun was real. It sat in the shop drawer for weeks, wrapped in an oilcloth.

One night in winter, Nadir would stand outside Mateo's house in the dark, the same gun cold in his pocket. The door would openhol and Mateo would step out, and then the little girl—Rosie—would run into his arms just as Nadir pulled the trigger. The click would be tiny, useless. Sahar had bought blanks. The child would look up, unhurt, and Nadir would lower the gun. An angel, he'd think.

The car was a Crown Vic. Trey and Kwame took it from the prosecutor Halstead outside an Italian restaurant, and Kwame laughed the whole way, slapping the dash. They ran down a shopkeeper named Pham two weeks later, dumped him outside a hospital like a bag of trash.

Voss would pick up Kwame hitchhiking on a cold road. Kwame would reach into his pocket—just for a cigarette—and Voss would shoot him twice. The body would burn with the car. Detective Isaiah Reece would stand over it by the roadside and recognize his brother's boots. Their mother would say, "You never once went looking for him," and Reece would have no answer.

Boyle pulled over the Hobarts for a taillight. He made Renee get out, groped her against the patrol car while Clay watched, hands shaking on the wheel, and then let them go with a warning. Voss asked the commander for a new patrol car that same afternoon.

Renee would be upside down in a burning wreck, the seatbelt pinning her. Boyle would crawl in through the shattered window, the same hands that had touched her, and drag her out by the shoulders. She'd cough smoke and look at him, and he'd look away.

Mateo changed the Halstead locks while Paula stood in the hallway, loud and afraid. "You're going to sell my keys to your gang, aren't you?" Mateo finished the job and left without a word.

Paula would fall down her stairs one cold evening. Her housekeeper Alba would find her. "You're the only friend I have," Paula would say, and Alba would help her up, saying nothing.

Mateo came to Nadir's shop next. He replaced the lock, but he warned: "The door itself is rotten. Replace it or you'll be broken into." Nadir accused him of running a con. That night, someone smashed the door in and stripped the shelves. The insurer refused to pay. The warning, they said, had been ignored.

Boyle pleaded with a health insurance clerk named Delia Frank for his father's treatment. She refused him twice, and he left with his fists in his pockets.

Clay would be stopped mid-carjacking of his own car, and Voss would talk the other officers out of shooting him. Then Clay would drive Trey away at speed and throw him out of the moving car onto the shoulder, where he'd roll and come up bloody.

Trey would find Pham's van packed with trafficked migrants, their wrists bound, and turn them loose at the docks. They'd scatter into the fog like birds.

In the first snow of the year, another collision would start another argument in the street. No one would remember any of this. The snow would cover everything.

Nadir waited until the night the first snow fell. He stood outside Mateo's house with the gun, and when the door opened, when the little girl ran into her father's arms, he pulled the trigger.

The click. The empty click.

The child looked up at him, unhurt.

Nadir lowered the gun. "Angel," he said.

Sahar had bought the blanks the same day they bought the gun, from a different store, in a different name. She'd known what he would do with it. She'd known he wouldn't need to.
